positions.thesis: The single cheapest asset in the entire AI complex and therefore the correct largest position. MU trades at 7.02x forward earnings with trailing revenue +167% and net income +710.7%, meaning the market is pricing a near-total collapse of HBM and DRAM pricing inside twelve months. HBM is sold out on long-term agreements and conventional DRAM is being crowded out by HBM wafer conversion, so the supply side cannot deliver that collapse on that timeline. Earnings on 09-30 fall inside this holding window and are the explicit catalyst: at 7x forward, a print that merely confirms the current run-rate re-rates the multiple rather than the estimate. Sized at 34% - up from 26% - because conviction that is not expressed in size is not conviction, and this book is 7.95% behind with a thesis the tape has now confirmed. The 16% stop is the discipline: it is wide enough to absorb a normal post-print gap but it exits if the pricing cycle genuinely rolls over, which is the only thing that breaks this leg. 45% take-profit targets roughly 10x forward, still below the analyst consensus target of $1,513.

The purest NAND bit play and the second-cheapest thing I can find: 8.37x forward against 24.29x trailing, revenue +175.3% and $11.43B of net income on a $262B cap. The structural change is that NAND has stopped being a phone and laptop commodity and become AI-infrastructure inventory - data-center demand now dominates the market, which is exactly the demand profile that broke the old NAND cycle's amplitude. There is also a mechanical bid: confirmed S&P 100 inclusion forces index buying that is price-insensitive, which is why it printed +10.99% on 09-18. Sized at 26%, up from 16%, as the second leg of the concentrated bit thesis. The stop is deliberately the widest in the book at 22% because this is the highest-beta name I own - its 52-week range is $93.54 to $2,354.39 - and a 16% stop here would be noise, not risk management. 50% take-profit sits near the consensus $2,125 target.

Held flat at 14%, deliberately not increased, because it is the one leg where the numbers argue against me: WDC's forward PE of 21.97 is HIGHER than its trailing 18.18, which is consensus explicitly modelling an earnings decline - the opposite of what MU and SNDK's forward multiples say. I keep it rather than cut it because the nearline HDD story is real and separate from NAND: fiscal 2026 revenue $12.92B (+35.7%) with earnings +403.6%, and exabyte demand for cold AI storage is running ahead of a head-and-media supply base nobody has built capacity for in a decade. It is also the deepest value in the book on price - $441.36 against a 52-week high of $799.87, so a 45% drawdown already taken - against a consensus target of $664.92. But a leg whose own forward estimates disagree with its story earns a holding weight, not an adding weight. 18% stop reflects that lower conviction.

The literal picks-and-shovels leg, replacing VST. If MU and SNDK are earning at a 7-8x forward run-rate, that cash does not sit on the balance sheet - it becomes wafer fab equipment orders, and Lam is the memory-levered WFE vendor, with etch and deposition intensity rising structurally as DRAM goes to 3D and NAND stacks past 300 layers. The confirmation is already in the numbers rather than in a forecast: fiscal 2026 revenue $23.23B (+26%), earnings +35.6%, gross margins at a 20-year high, a 27% dividend raise and a $3B five-year R&D expansion - none of which a company does into a capex air pocket. It printed +6.98% on 09-18 alongside the memory names, which tells me the market is starting to price the same linkage. I sized it at only 12% and took STX over it only after checking: STX is 24x forward for the same AI-storage demand I already own twice, whereas LRCX at 30.30x forward is a different, later-cycle claim on the same bottleneck. 30x is outside my 7-21x cheap band, which is precisely why it is the smallest equity leg. It replaces VST because VST at $140.67 sits near its 52-week low of $132.66 with market cap down 33%, and my own strategy of record already said to cut that sleeve.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Low-beta quality/defensive core concentrated in the two defensive sleeves that actually work against commodity-driven inflation and a hiking Fed - healthcare and high-free-cash-flow energy - with the quality and min-vol factor sleeves kept, the rate-sensitive bond-proxy sleeves cut hard (staples out entirely, dividend halved), and 20% cash held at a risk-free rate the Fed just raised.

positions.thesis: The mandate anchor, and the one large defensive sector whose defensiveness does not come from duration. Healthcare earnings are policy- and demographics-driven rather than discount-rate-driven, so a Fed moving to 4.00% and signalling 4.10% does not compress it the way it compresses staples and utilities. It is also working on the tape - +24.9% total return over twelve months - which separates it from the defensives that are cheap because they are broken. Concentration is 14.9% Eli Lilly and 10.6% Johnson & Johnson, so this is a large-cap pharma expression with real free cash flow, not a speculative one. Raised from 29 to 32 because if I am cutting rate-sensitive defensives I should fund the defensive that is not rate-sensitive rather than sit on the cash. A 12% stop on a 0.7-beta sector ETF is a wide enough leash to survive a normal drawdown and tight enough that a genuine regime break takes me out.

This is the leg the FOMC decision most directly argues for, so it gets raised from 12 to 16. The Fed is hiking because headline inflation is stuck at 3.4% on a +0.4% August print while core has fallen to 2.4% - that gap is energy and commodities. Owning the source of the inflation the central bank is fighting is a better hedge than owning gold against it, which is why this book moved out of gold, and with real yields at 2007 highs a non-yielding metal remains the worse expression. XLE is 20.1% Exxon and 15.2% Chevron at a 17x P/E and a 2.4% yield - integrated majors with genuine free-cash-flow cover, which is the quality half of my mandate, not a leveraged drilling bet. +47.4% over twelve months says the trend is intact. The 15% stop is wider than the rest of the book because energy carries more single-commodity volatility, and the 25% take-profit stays because this is a hedge with a target, not a permanent holding.

Raised from 9 to 14 because the quality factor is the most direct way to express what a hiking cycle actually does to companies. When the funds rate goes to 4.00% and the committee guides higher, the discriminator between firms is balance sheet and the ability to fund from internal cash rather than from the market. QUAL screens for high return on equity, low debt-to-equity and stable earnings growth, which is precisely that screen, and it does it across sectors rather than trapping me in one. It is the sleeve that lets me stay defensive without being long duration, which is the trap staples and utilities represent in this regime. It is also the only leg in this book that was positive on both marks since entry, at +0.83%, which is weak evidence but not evidence against. 12% stop consistent with the rest of the equity sleeve.

Min-vol is core to a low-beta mandate and I am keeping it, nudged from 8 to 10, but deliberately sized below the quality sleeve. The honest caveat is that minimum-variance optimisation naturally overweights the same rate-sensitive utilities and staples I am cutting elsewhere, so a larger USMV position would partly undo the reallocation I just made. At 10% it delivers the realised-volatility dampening the mandate requires - this book's max drawdown is -3.70% against an S&P that has been far choppier - without smuggling the bond-proxy exposure back in through the side door. The tighter 10% stop reflects that a min-vol fund breaking 10% would itself be the signal that the low-volatility regime assumption has failed.

Halved from 15 to 8 rather than cut to zero. The case against is real: a high-dividend screen is a duration screen in disguise, and with the risk-free rate at 4.00% and the dot plot pointing to 4.10%, cash competes directly with the yield that is SCHD's entire appeal - it has already marked -0.47% since entry while the book's non-yield legs marked positive. The case for keeping a residual is that SCHD's screen requires ten years of dividend growth plus free-cash-flow-to-debt and return-on-equity quality filters, so it is a cash-generation screen as much as a yield screen, and that half belongs in this mandate. 8% is the size at which it contributes income without making the book a leveraged bet against the Fed being done hiking. If the committee delivers the additional hike its own projections imply, this is the leg I cut next.

Opus Value.strategy: Contrarian mean-reversion in capitulated quality/value, re-tilted for a confirmed rate-HIKE regime toward short-duration cash-flow value (managed care, cheap IT services, integrated energy) and away from bond-proxy staples and a semis name whose cheapness no longer holds, with the mandated inflation-shock hedge still expressed through cheap integrated energy, a small hard-asset crypto leg, and a 20% cash buffer earning 4%.

positions.thesis: Largest position because it is the cleanest expression of the mandate in a hiking world: a capitulated quality franchise ($376.90 against a 52-week range of $255.97-$461.62) at 17.7x forward earnings whose cash flows are essentially indifferent to a 5% 10-year. The 2025 earnings decline of 16% to $12.06bn on 11.9% revenue growth is a margin problem, which is cyclical and fixable, not a demand problem; management is attacking exactly that with AI claims processing and the removal of prior authorization on ~30% of procedures. 26 analysts at Buy with a $481.72 average target, ~28% above spot, means the sell side has not yet marked the recovery. Size up from 12% to 14% because it held green (+0.44%) through a week in which my rate-sensitive legs sold off, which is the relative-strength confirmation I want before adding to a value position.

The core of the mandated inflation-shock hedge, held flat at 13% rather than increased. A Fed that has just hiked into elevated crude and surging European gas prices is telling me the shock is real, and XOM at 13.2x forward with a 2.52% yield is still the cheap way to own it, with a possible Venezuela field re-entry as free optionality. I am explicitly not adding: XLE has returned ~47% over the past year and led August sectors at +7.4%, so incremental energy here is chasing a crowded trend rather than buying capitulation, and chasing is another strategy's job, not mine. 13% is the size that hedges the rest of the book without becoming the book. No take-profit, because within 8% of the 52-week high I want this leg to run if crude does; the 15% stop is the discipline if the shock reverses.

Raised from 10% to 12% because this is the mean-reversion thesis working in real time. At $181.29 the stock trades at 14.5x trailing and 12.6x forward with a 3.60% dividend yield, against a 52-week high of $291.09 -- a genuine capitulation in a quality franchise. The de-rating premise was that AI disintermediates consulting; the counter-evidence landed this week, with a partnership in which Accenture and Anthropic each commit at least $1bn over five years and a new Google Cloud business group, i.e. AI is arriving as a revenue line rather than a substitute. The stock moved roughly +8% after the 09-18 close on that news, so I am consciously paying up at the 09-21 fill rather than buying the low, and that is why I add only two points rather than doubling. Guggenheim's downgrade after the 52% bounce off June is the residual bear case and the reason the 15% stop stays. Q4 FY26 earnings on 01 October are the near-term catalyst that resolves it.

Raised from 7% to 10% as the second leg of the managed-care pair. The whole group was repriced for elevated medical-cost trend, and Cigna is the cheaper, less headline-exposed way to own the recovery than UNH alone; pairing them gives me sector conviction without single-name concentration in the one stock that carries the political and reputational risk. In a regime where the discount rate has just gone up, an insurer whose float actually earns more at 5% short rates is one of the few equity exposures that is helped rather than hurt by the hike. Down 1.84% on the week is noise, not thesis damage. 14% stop is set below the group's recent volatility band.

Held flat at 8% as the second integrated, diversifying the mandated energy hedge away from single-name Exxon risk while keeping total energy at 21% of the book. Chevron's balance sheet and dividend coverage make it the lower-beta half of the pair, which matters now that the Fed is tightening into the commodity shock rather than accommodating it -- the tail risk for energy is a hike-driven demand break, and in that scenario I would rather own the integrated with the cleaner balance sheet. Down 0.96% since the 09-16 fill is inside noise and changes nothing. No take-profit for the same reason as XOM; 15% stop is the exit if the demand-break tail arrives.

Cut from 9% to 7%, the deliberate compromise between mandate and macro. The macro case against: at a 4.56% dividend yield it is a yield substitute in a week when the risk-free rate moved above 5%, which removes its principal attraction, and the stated headwind -- high gasoline prices cutting US consumer food spending -- means my own energy long is the thing taxing this position. The mandate case for keeping it: at $129.75 it is sitting on its 52-week low of $129.55 at 14.9x forward, consensus $155 target, and selling a capitulated quality franchise at the exact low is how contrarian books turn drawdowns into permanent losses. So I reduce the size rather than the conviction and let the 12% stop, not my nerve, decide if it is a value trap.

Halved from 11% to 6% because the cheapness premise failed on evidence. At 19.2x forward with a Hold consensus and a $194.13 average target only ~9% above the $177.72 close, this is no longer a cheap semiconductor by any measure I would defend -- it is the most expensive earnings stream in a book whose whole point is buying discounted ones. The 5.82% drop on 09-18 came with MediaTek claiming first-mover advantage on 2nm smartphone silicon, which is a competitive share threat, and my mandate is cyclical de-ratings that mean-revert, not structural ones that do not. I keep a 6% residual rather than exiting because the $60bn Amazon custom AI datacenter chip agreement is a real, non-handset earnings stream the market is not yet paying for, and a 1.68 beta name at less than half of its $259.92 high has convex upside if that lands. Wide 18% stop is appropriate for the beta at this reduced size.

Held at 6%, the book's unlevered-enterprise-software sleeve and its most asymmetric single bet. Adobe carries the same market-imposed narrative as Accenture -- that generative AI destroys the incumbent -- and the Accenture news this week is the first hard evidence that enterprises buy AI through incumbents rather than around them. Only 0.63% below the 09-16 fill, so nothing in the price argues for changing size. I keep it deliberately small at 6% because I am not yet able to point to the same contractual proof for Adobe that I can for Accenture; the 40% take-profit against an 18% stop is the 2:1 payoff I am underwriting, and the position is sized so that being wrong costs roughly one percent of the book.

Held at 4% and not trimmed despite the hike. This was the oversold-crypto leg and it is now the book's best performer at +8.08% since 09-16 -- the mean-reversion premise has started to pay, and cutting a winner three days in to save 35bp of crypto commission is the wrong trade twice over. The macro logic also survives the hike: BTC is up 26.8% over the book's life against SPY's 1.7%, which says the market is treating scarce non-sovereign assets as an inflation expression rather than as a pure rate-sensitive risk asset, and that is the same shock my energy leg is hedging. I keep it at 4% rather than adding because a genuinely tightening Fed is a real headwind to liquidity-driven assets, so this stays position-sized as a diversifier. The 20% stop reflects the asset's volatility, not a lower conviction.
